readerTitle: The line around the block that sank three stores
caseNote: 가상 사례 (리필 생활용품 매장, 일정 관리 앱) + 실제 연구 (Startup Genome 2011 보고서, 수치 없이 일반적으로만 인용)
insight: 성장에 쓰는 돈은 지금 있는 것을 키울 뿐 고치지 않는다. 그래서 키우기 전에 고객이 스스로 돌아오는지, 판매 한 건이 돈을 남기는지부터 확인한다.
misconception: 줄이 길고 매출이 계획보다 높으면 빨리 확장할수록 좋다. 확장하면서 문제를 고치면 된다.

sources.text: Startup Genome Project (Marmer, Herrmann, Dogrultan, Berman), Startup Genome Report Extra on Premature Scaling, 2011
리필 매장과 일정 관리 앱 사례 및 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Startup Genome 2011 보고서가 '수천 개 스타트업'을 분석했고 조기 확장이 실패한 스타트업에서 가장 흔한 패턴이라고 보고한 점을 원문으로 확인하세요. 흔히 인용되는 '74%' 같은 수치는 정확한 정의와 표본을 확인하기 전까지 카드에 넣지 않았습니다.
3번 카드 차트의 주간 방문객 수(620 → 540 → 380 → 310 → 300)는 가상 수치입니다. 오픈 효과가 빠지고 재방문 고객 수준에서 안정되는 모양을 보여주기 위한 설명용입니다.
8번 카드의 가입 4,000명, 영업 인력 8명, 월 광고비 $50,000는 모두 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: The line went around the block.
body: A new refill shop opens on a busy street. People bring empty bottles and fill them with soap, shampoo and cleaner by weight.
In week one, the line runs out the door. Neighbors post photos. The owner starts looking at two more locations before the first month is over.

image.label: A long line of shoppers holding empty bottles outside a small shop
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 작은 리필 매장 앞에 빈 병을 든 사람들이 길게 줄 서 있음. 매장 안쪽에서 주인이 부동산 전단지 두 장을 들여다보는 모습. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A landlord offers two more spots.
body: Three weeks in, sales are triple your plan. A landlord offers two more shops across town on five-year leases, but only if you sign this month.

options.text: Sign both. Demand like this won't wait
options.feedback: You lock in the spots before rivals do. But you commit five years of rent based on three weeks of opening buzz.

options.text: Sign one, pass on the other
options.feedback: Half the risk, and you still grow. But you are still betting on numbers you haven't tested yet.

options.text: Pass for now. Track how many first-month customers come back
options.feedback: You may lose these two spots. In return, you learn whether the line was real demand or just novelty before you multiply it.

cards.title: The buzz faded. The rent didn't.
body: In this version of the story, the owner signed both leases. Then the opening crowd thinned out and settled at the level of real repeat customers.
The first shop still covers its costs. The two new ones were sized for the launch-month line, and both lose money every week.

groups.label: Weekly customers at the first shop

cards.title: Premature scaling
body: **Premature scaling** means spending to grow, with more locations, staff, stock or marketing, before you have proven the business works at its current size.

The key idea: growth spending **multiplies what you already have**. If customers come back and each sale makes money, scaling multiplies that. If not, it multiplies the problem, and adds fixed costs on top.

image.label: A small cracked block being copied into three larger cracked blocks
image.brief: 개념 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에 금이 간 작은 블록 하나, 화살표 "Scale"를 지나 오른쪽에 같은 금이 더 크게 보이는 블록 세 개. 금이 커지는 점을 강조. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Three questions before you grow.
body: A 2011 Startup Genome report studied thousands of startups and found premature scaling was the most common pattern among those that failed. Before spending to grow, check:
list: **Do customers come back on their own?** Repeat visits, not opening crowds
**Does each sale leave money** after the costs that come with it?
**Does it run without you?** Can someone else open the second shop?
cards.callout: If the answer to any is "not yet," growth spending will hide the problem, not solve it.

cards.title: The same trap, in other clothes.
body: A food maker sells out its first 2,000 jars, mostly to friends and local fans. It orders 50,000 jars and a bigger kitchen. Stores reorder slowly.
A distributor wins one large client and leases a second warehouse. The client leaves a year later.
Each looks like a growth decision. Each is really a bet that early signals will last. The cost lands in commitments that are hard to undo: leases, salaries, stock.

cards.title: Waiting has a cost too.
body: Some markets reward speed. A rival can take the best location, or the customers you hoped to win.
So the rule is not "grow slowly." It's "grow on evidence." The fix is often to make growth cheaper to reverse: a pop-up before a lease, contractors before hires, a small ad test before a big budget.
Once the three questions get a clear yes, holding back becomes the risky choice.

cards.title: Now it's a scheduling app.
body: Your scheduling app hit the top of a popular launch site. 4,000 users signed up in one week.
An investor suggests hiring eight salespeople and spending $50,000 a month on ads. What do you do first?

options.text: Hire and spend now, while attention is high
options.feedback: You ride the wave. But launch-week signups are like the opening-day line, and you'd be paying salaries before knowing who stays.

options.text: Watch how many week-one users are still active in week six, then raise ad spend in steps
options.feedback: You give up some momentum. You gain proof that users stay, so each ad dollar grows something that lasts.

options.text: Skip the hires but start the full ad budget
options.feedback: Ads are easier to stop than salaries, which helps. But you'd still be buying users before knowing if they stick.

cards.title: Scaling multiplies what you have. Prove it first.
body: Before adding locations, people or ad spend, check that customers return on their own and that each sale leaves money.
**Try it today:** look at your customers from three months ago. How many have come back since? Write that number down before your next growth decision.
